title: Beyond ‘local is best’: Multi‐source seed mixes can provide additional benefits in grassland restoration
content:
Our results support that local seed mixes can ensure high initial establishment of seeded species, even in climates this region may experience in the future. However, multi-source mixes including the local source can result in comparable establishment rates to when the local source is sown alone and produce populations with more trait variation, potentially increasing adaptive potential. Maintaining local sources of seed remains important, but alternative seed sourcing strategies may improve restoration success in an uncertain future.


Abstract

A key decision in restoration planning is where to obtain seeds from to establish native plant populations. The most widespread practice, local seed provenancing, assumes that seed sourced near restoration sites will perform best, yet outcomes are often variable. To improve establishment, two alternatives have been proposed that include multiple sources to increase genetic diversity and broaden adaptation to environmental conditions. Admixture provenancing supplements the local source with nearby sources to boost genetic diversity while minimizing maladaptation risk, whereas climate-adjusted provenancing combines a local source with those from climates we predict the restoration site will experience in the future. Since these strategies have rarely been compared to one another in a field setting, their relative effectiveness, including how many additional sources are needed to influence establishment, remains largely unexplored. We conducted an experimental tallgrass prairie restoration to test how seed mix design, including (1) seed provenance, (2) the number of sources and (3) seed provenancing strategy (local, admixture or climate-adjusted) influenced sown species richness, abundance and flowering phenology. We also investigated (4) whether some seed mixes outperform others in experimentally warmed conditions. Among single-source mixes, local sources had the highest sown richness compared to regional sources and those from predicted future climates, and this resulted in a shift in community composition. However, the local source was not the best-establishing source for every species. When sources were combined in multi-source seed mixes, establishment was similar across all sourcing strategies. Mixes with at least two sources, especially climate-adjusted mixes, produced more flowering individuals across the growing season compared to the local source. All sources performed equally well under warming. Synthesis and applications. Our results support that local seed mixes can ensure high initial establishment of seeded species, even in climates this region may experience in the future. However, multi-source mixes including the local source can result in comparable establishment rates to when the local source is sown alone and produce populations with more trait variation, potentially increasing adaptive potential. Maintaining local sources of seed remains important, but alternative seed sourcing strategies may improve restoration success in an uncertain future.
